Patient 1 was a 47-year-old woman
who presented with a subacute, severe pancerebellar syn-
drome. Brain magnetic resonance (MR) was normal and
CSF analysis showed 40 white cells. Two months later, an
adenocarcinoma of probable breast origin was demon-
strated in an axillary adenopathy. Four years later, she was
tumor free but very disabled from the cerebellar syndrome.
Patient 2 was a 42-year-old woman who developed a severe
cerebellar syndrome 1 month after diagnosis of breast can-
cer. Brain MR was normal and CSF analysis showed 10
white cells. Two years later, she was tumor free and neuro-
logically stable. 
Among the other 5 patients, 4 presented a favorable
evolution related to treatment of the tumor (see Table 2,

Patients 4, 5, 6, 7). These patients had a mild to moderate
cerebellar syndrome weeks to months before the diagno-
sis of breast cancer. They all had normal MR, and the cere-
bellar syndrome improved after removal of the tumor.
Patient 3 (see Table 2) was considered to be possibly para-
neoplastic as she did not improve after tumor treatment.
She had cerebellar atrophy in the initial MR and the clin-
ical picture was similar to that of idiopathic cerebellar de-
generation. 
Sensory-predominant neuropathy
We included in this group 17 (18%) patients in whom
sensory symptoms were the initial complaint and re-
mained isolated or clearly predominant during most of the
clinical course. Patients who showed minor motor weak-
ness or only neurophysiologic motor involvement were in-
cluded in this group. Five patients were positive for Hu-ab
(3 breast, 2 ovary), 2 had amphyphisin-ab (2 breast), 1 had
an atypical antibody (ovary), and 9 had no detectable
antibodies (7 breast, 1 ovary, 1 cervix). The clinical picture
of those patients with Hu-ab, atypical antibody, and
amphiphysin-ab resembled that of patients with Hu-ab,
small cell lung cancer, and sensory neuropathy with pre-
dominant involvement of vibratory and joint position
senses and asymmetric onset (41). The serum of the patient
with the atypical antibody immunoreacted with the neu-
ronal cytoplasm in a pattern different from that described
in a patient with chronic, asymmetric, ataxic sensory neu-
ropathy and breast cancer, whose serum reacted with the
posterior gray horn of the spinal cord (30). All the seropos-
itive patients had an isolated sensory neuropathy with clin-
ical features (asymmetric onset, early involvement of
hands, sensory ataxia) and electromyography (EMG) fea-
tures (absent sensory nerve action potentials with normal
motor nerve conduction velocities in the 5 studies re-
viewed) compatible with primary involvement of the dor-
sal root ganglia (neuronopathy) (13).
The clinical picture and evolution of the 9 seronega-
tive patients was heterogeneous (Table 3). Five patients
(see Table 3, Patients 1, 5, 6, 7, 8) had a large ﬁber sensory
neuropathy with predominant gait ataxia. Four of them
had atypical features for seropositive sensory neuropathy,
2 patients improved, another developed a severe motor
deﬁcit over the ensuing years, and 1 patient had a demy-
elinating neuropathy. Two patients (see Table 3, Patients 3
and 4) presented with paresthesias and itching in the lower
limbs 5 and 9 months before breast cancer was diagnosed
(46). Lastly, Patients 2 and 9 were considered to have pos-
sible paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy because they had
less speciﬁc sensory symptoms (numbness and paresthe-
sias) and did not improve after treatment of the tumor.
Sensorimotor neuropathy
Four patients (4.3%) presented with peripheral neu-
ropathy and predominant motor impairment considered to
be possible PNS associated with breast cancer. Two patients
developed an acute sensorimotor neuropathy fulﬁlling the
criteria for Guillain Barré syndrome, 1 coincident with and
the other 4 months after diagnosis of breast cancer. Two pa-
tients presented a neuropathy with the features of chronic id-
iopathic demyelinating polyneuropathy 9 months before
and 5 months after the diagnosis of breast cancer, respec-
tively. EMG studies suggested a chronic demyelinating
polyradiculoneuropathy in both patients, and a nerve biopsy
performed in 1 demonstrated inﬂammatory and demyelin-

ating features. CSF analysis showed elevated protein content
in both (0.53 and 1.20 g/L, respectively), and hypercellular-
ity in 1 (19 white cells with 84% lymphocytes). Clinical evo-
lution was progressive in 1 and remitting-relapsing in the
other. Both patients responded to plasmapheresis.

Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
Four patients presented with opsoclonus-myoclonus
syndrome. Three patients had breast cancer (2 with Ri-ab)
and 1 ovarian carcinoma. No clinical differences were ob-
served between Ri-ab-negative and Ri-ab-positive patients
with breast cancer. The patient with ovarian cancer devel-
oped opsoclonus without myoclonus 2 months after tumor
diagnosis and after a second cycle of carboplatin, taxol,
and topotecan. The syndrome did not improve and the pa-
tient died from tumor progression 4 months later.
Other neurologic syndromes
Seven patients were considered to have deﬁnitive
PNS associated with breast cancer. Three patients pre-
sented with multifocal involvement of the nervous system
(encephalomyelitis) associated with Ri-ab. Two of them
had a predominant brainstem syndrome with ophthal-
moparesis, dysarthria, tremor, and axial or pancerebellar
syndrome but no opsoclonus. Dorsal bulboprotuberantial,
bilateral, and symmetric hyperintense lesions on T2-
weighted MR images were observed in 1 of the patients.
The third Ri-ab-positive patient presented with a progres-
sive paraparesia with abolished deep tendon reﬂexes and
a T9 sensory level. She subsequently developed weakness
in the upper limbs, urinary incontinence, dysarthria, and
postural tremor in the head and both arms. EMG showed
denervation in the 4 limbs without bulbar involvement.
Spinal and brain MR were normal. A breast adenocarci-
noma was diagnosed 8 months after the onset of neuro-
logic symptoms. 
Two patients had cancer-associated retinopathy.
Antirecoverin or other antiretinal antibodies were not
measured. One patient developed a typical stiff-person
syndrome (positive for amphiphysin-ab, negative for
GAD-ab), and another presented with limbic encephalitis
deﬁned by clinical and MR features 3 months before the
diagnosis of breast cancer. 
Lastly, 3 seronegative patients with breast cancer
were considered as possible paraneoplastic. Two had
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The third patient presented
a subacute cerebellar syndrome with multicranial nerve in-
volvement (right VI and VII and bilateral XII nerve
palsies) and bilateral Babinski sign. An axillary lymph
node biopsy revealed an adenocarcinoma 2 months after
the onset of the neurologic symptoms. Distal paresthesias
and amyotrophy appeared during evolution, and elec-
trophysiologic studies revealed an axonal sensory-
predominant neuropathy. She did not improve after treat-
ment of the tumor.
In summary, all patients with gynecologic cancer
presented with deﬁnitive PNS, and onconeural antibodies
were diagnosed in 93% of them. In contrast, 20% of PNSs
associated with breast cancer were deﬁned as possible and
the incidence of onconeural antibodies was 51%, exclud-
ing the 2 patients with paraneoplastic retinopathy in whom
antiretinal antibodies were not analyzed.
